title: Toil Reduction & Automation
summary: Turning the "reduce toil" principle into a concrete, ongoing practice rather than a slogan.

slides.markdown:
**Toil** is manual, repetitive, automatable work with no lasting value. Reducing it isn't a one-time project — it's a **ladder** you keep climbing.

- Identify it precisely, don't just call anything annoying "toil."
- Climb the automation ladder one rung at a time: manual → documented → scripted → self-service → eliminated.
- Measure it, or you can't tell if you're actually winning.

Toil has five specific traits: **manual** (a human does it by hand), **repetitive** (it recurs, not one-off), **automatable** (a machine could do it), **tactical** (reactive, not strategic), and **no enduring value** (doing it again next week looks identical, it doesn't make the system better).

A novel, one-time investigation isn't toil — it fails the repetitive test. Writing a design doc isn't toil — it fails manual/automatable and has lasting value. The test filters out "work I don't enjoy" from "work that should be automated."

slides.subTitle: Five rungs from manual to gone
slides.markdown:
![The automation ladder: manual, documented, scripted, self-service, eliminated](assets/automation-ladder.svg)

Most toil doesn't jump straight from manual to eliminated — it climbs: first someone documents the steps (a runbook), then scripts them, then makes the script self-service so the requester doesn't need the on-call engineer at all, and finally the underlying cause is fixed so the task disappears entirely.

assets.alt: The automation ladder: manual, documented, scripted, self-service, eliminated

slides.markdown:
Google's SRE model caps toil-like operational work at roughly **50%** of an SRE's time, with the rest protected for engineering — building automation, improving systems, doing the work that actually reduces future toil.

The cap matters because toil, left unchecked, expands to fill all available time — there's always one more manual task that feels urgent. A hard ceiling forces the team to actually schedule automation work instead of perpetually deferring it for the next fire.

slides.subTitle: A ticket automated away
slides.markdown:
A recurring ticket: "restart service X and clear its cache" arrives 3–4 times a week, always resolved the same way by whoever's on-call. First rung: someone writes a script that does both steps in one command — cuts resolution time but still needs a human to run it.

Next rung: the script gets wired into a self-service bot so the requester triggers it directly, no on-call needed. Eventually, someone finds and fixes the actual cache-staleness bug — the ticket stops arriving at all. Each rung removed real toil; only the last one removed the root cause.

slides.subTitle: Automating a bad process
slides.markdown:
Automating a process before questioning whether it should exist just makes the bad process run **faster and more invisibly** — you've locked in the waste instead of removing it. If a manual approval step exists because of a policy no one remembers the reason for, scripting that approval away can quietly reintroduce the risk the policy was for.

The correct order: first ask "should this happen at all, or less often," then "can it be simplified," and only then "how do we automate what's left." Automation should compress a good process, not fossilize a bad one.
